meta.title: Who really said "Actor: A Guy Who If You Ain't Talking About Him, He Ain't Listening"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Brando said it for years, but Ed Sullivan printed it in 1955 as a joke Brando had just collected. Credited to publicist George Glass; in print by 1951.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Actor: A Guy Who If You Ain't Talking About Him, He Ain't Listening'?
meta.ogDescription: Ed Sullivan printed it in 1955 as a gag Brando had just collected. The credit goes to Hollywood publicist George Glass — and a 1951 version has no name.

answer.label: Not Brando’s coinage — credited to publicist George Glass
answer.authorDates: 1910–1984 · Hollywood publicist and producer — credited from 1966; the earliest printed instance (1951) carries no name
answer.sourceLine: Brando genuinely used the line — Ed Sullivan printed it in June 1955 as a gag Brando had just added to his file of jokes about actors, and The Observer of London was hanging it directly on him by the end of that year. But Quote Investigator ↗ found the thought in print in 1951 with no name attached, and by 1966 the credit had settled on Hollywood publicist George Glass — whom Brando’s 1973 biographer named as the man Brando got it from.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: Collier’s, 21 July 1951 — Gladwin Hill on Kirk Douglas, speaker unnamed, softer wording
Ed Sullivan, “Little Old New York,” 10 June 1955 — listed as a joke he had just added
Mike Connolly, “Off the Grapevine,” The Toledo Blade, 26 September 1966

source.excerpt: Marlon Brando has a file of jokes about actors. He just added this one: “An actor is a guy, who, if you ain’t talking about him, ain’t listening.”
trail: July 1951 — the earliest instance Quote Investigator located ↗ ran in Collier’s, where an unnamed acquaintance used the idea to skewer Kirk Douglas — no “ain’t,” and no author.
June 1955 — Ed Sullivan’s column reported that Brando kept a file of jokes about actors and had just added this one, as QI transcribes it ↗. Sullivan pointedly did not call it Brando’s.
Late 1955 — The Observer of London printed the familiar wording and hung it straight on Brando; Wikiquote ↗ still carries it among his quotes, sourced to that paper.

1966–1973 — columnist Mike Connolly named publicist George Glass as the author, and Bob Thomas’s 1973 Brando biography said Brando picked it up from Glass; Wikipedia’s article on Glass ↗ notes that several reference works, including the Yale Book of Quotations, credit him.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest printing that puts the line in Brando’s mouth — and it is also the reason the authorship claim fails. Sullivan presents it as inventory Brando collected, not as something Brando said first; the wording also differs slightly from the version that later circulated under his name — Sullivan’s printing drops the “he” before “ain’t listening.”
source.rightsNote: This is a spoken Hollywood wisecrack whose author is unresolved: the earliest printing Quote Investigator found ↗ (1951) carries no name, and the credit to George Glass first appears in print in 1966. Every documented appearance sits in a magazine, newspaper column or book published in 1951 or later, so nothing here is old enough to be public domain and we assert no rights status.

author.name: George Glass
author.heading: The press agent behind the line
author.bio: George Glass was an American film publicist and producer who became one of the most quotable operators in postwar Hollywood. He was head publicist and an associate producer at Stanley Kramer’s independent company, where his campaigns for Champion and Home of the Brave helped make its reputation, and he later joined Marlon Brando’s Pennebaker Productions as an executive producer on films including One-Eyed Jacks and Paris Blues. That proximity is the whole story of this quote: the press agent supplied the wisecrack, and the movie star supplied the megaphone.

Credited to George Glass: Mike Connolly, “Off the Grapevine,” The Toledo Blade, September 26, 1966. misattribution.heading: Who gets credited, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote — it is a real wisecrack with the wrong name on it. Brando is the reason you know the line, not the reason it exists.

items.why: Brando used it constantly, but the columnist who first printed it in his mouth was careful not to give it to him: Ed Sullivan wrote in June 1955 ↗ that Brando kept a file of jokes about actors and had just added this one. Brando himself later wondered aloud in print who had said it.

Wikiquote ↗ lists it in Brando’s main Quotes section sourced only to The Observer, and Goodreads ↗ carries it as Brando’s with no citation at all, under its own notice that community-added quotes are unverified. Neither records that the line predates his use of it.
The Weekly World News printed the line under Boy George’s name in January 2006, as QI documents ↗ — a clean illustration of an unowned quip migrating to whoever is famous.

misattribution.truthLine: Best available answer: a Hollywood press agent’s line, credited to George Glass from 1966 onward and named as Brando’s source by his own 1973 biographer — though Quote Investigator ↗ stops short of calling Glass the definite originator, because a nameless 1951 version came first.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Brando
lead: A joke about actors needs a famous actor attached to it, and in 1955 there was no more famous actor alive. Ed Sullivan’s column that June reported the line as inventory — Brando kept a file of gags about his own profession, and this was the newest one in it. Within months The Observer in London had printed the familiar wording with Brando’s name on the end of it, and the joke stopped being a joke Brando told and became a joke Brando made.

The rival claim is the more Hollywood story. George Glass was a press agent: producing quotable lines for other people to say was literally his job, and he supplied them to Kramer’s company and later to Brando’s own. When Brando publicly wondered in 1966 who had said it, Mike Connolly answered in print ↗ that it was Glass — and threw in a second Glass line about actors for good measure.
context.detailsSummary: The 1951 version, and where it points
detailsBody: The 1951 Collier’s instance is not the quip in its punchy form. It is an acquaintance describing Kirk Douglas — no “ain’t,” no definition-of-an-actor framing, and no attribution to anyone. QI treats it as the earliest appearance of the idea rather than as a rival author, which is why nobody, including this page, can say who first sharpened it into the version people quote.

The line kept drifting after Brando. A 1964 newspaper piece about Lee Marvin ran it with no name at all as something “often said,” a 1966 columnist called it an old saw, and by 2006 the Weekly World News had reassigned it to Boy George — a useful reminder that an unowned wisecrack will attach itself to whoever is famous at the time.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI's earliest located instance is Gladwin Hill's 21 July 1951 Collier's profile of Kirk Douglas, spoken by an unnamed acquaintance without 'ain't'; Ed Sullivan's 10 June 1955 column said Brando kept a file of jokes about actors and had just added this one; The Observer (London) printed it credited to Brando later in 1955; Mike Connolly credited producer George Glass on 26 September 1966 in the Toledo Blade; Bob Thomas's 1973 biography (p. 55) says Brando learned it from publicist George Glass and quoted it many times; Weekly World News reassigned it to Boy George in 2006; QI concludes Brando was the primary vector for popularization but it is unclear whether Glass originated it.

Wikiquote lists 'An actor's a guy, who if you ain't talking about him, ain't listening.' in Marlon Brando's main Quotes section, sourced to The Observer, and gives Brando's dates as 3 April 1924 – 1 July 2004.

Wikipedia's article on George Glass gives his dates as 19 August 1910 – 1 April 1984, describes him as an American film producer and publicist who was head publicist and associate producer for Stanley Kramer's independent company (campaigns for Champion and Home of the Brave) and later an executive producer at Brando's Pennebaker Productions; its Quotations section states Glass is credited by several sources, including the Yale Book of Quotations, with originating the witticism, and that the line has also been attributed to Brando, who reportedly heard it from Glass and quoted it many times.
Marlon Brando was an American actor, born 3 April 1924 and died 1 July 2004, who won Best Actor Oscars for On the Waterfront and The Godfather and formed his own production company, Pennebaker.

Goodreads carries 'An actor's a guy who, if you ain't talking about him, ain't listening.' attributed to Marlon Brando with no source citation, under a notice that quotes are added by the community and are not verified by Goodreads.
Internet Archive holds a scan of 'Marlon, portrait of the rebel as an artist' by Bob Thomas, Random House, New York, 1973; the item is access-restricted.
